before: The journey towards God is an inward one, worked out in the self.
after: The journey towards God is inward and is worked out in the self.

before: The path leads in turn to the truth (*haqiqa*), the reality that is seen once the path has been walked.
after: The path leads in turn to the truth (*haqiqa*), which is the reality seen once the path has been walked.

where: § The inner never cancels the outer, ¶2
before: The lie is in the claim to be a true ʿarif, one who knows God.
after: The lie is in the claim to be a true ʿarif who knows God.

where: § The inner never cancels the outer, ¶7 (the wudu story)
before: One day, as he was making his ritual ablution (*wudu*), his disciples suddenly fell into prostration, glorifying God.
after: One day, as he was making his ritual ablution (*wudu*), his disciples suddenly fell into prostration and glorified God.

before: The path purifies the way we practise the law, giving each act more depth each time it is done.
after: The path purifies the way we practise the law and gives each act more depth each time it is done.

before: Worship does have stages, and the *Kernel* finds one true sense in the talk of release, though not the sense its proponents intend.
after: Worship does have stages, and the *Kernel* finds in the talk of release one true sense that its proponents do not intend.
note: Fix 1 (folded). The proponents' contrast is kept.

before: Acts of worship develop the soul, bringing its capacities "from potentiality to actuality" [@kernel, p. 30], that is, making real what was only possible.
after: Acts of worship develop the soul and bring its capacities "from potentiality to actuality" [@kernel, p. 30], which means making real what was only possible.
note: Fix 1 for the participle ("and bring"), fix 2 for the gloss ("which means").

before: Nothing inward stands in for the law, and the inner work begins inside it, with attention in prayer.
after: Nothing inward stands in for the law, and the inner work begins inside it with attention in prayer.

before: For one prayer each day this week, keep its time free, with nothing planned straight after it.
after: For one prayer each day this week, keep its time free and plan nothing straight after it.

where: § The inner never cancels the outer, ¶2
before: The person works these wonders for their own desires, and what they do is not a wonder of the friends of God (*karama*) but magic (*sihr*).
after: The person works these wonders for their own desires, and what they do is magic (*sihr*) rather than a wonder of the friends of God (*karama*).
note: "Not X but Y" → "rather than" (D53). The lecturer's contrast is kept.

where: § The inner never cancels the outer, ¶8
before: There the states a traveller passes through, and the lights that appear from time to time, are called "a preliminary to an enduring condition" [@kernel, p. 30].
after: There Tabatabaʾi calls the states a traveller passes through, and the lights that appear from time to time, "a preliminary to an enduring condition" [@kernel, p. 30].
note: Source named as the actor in place of the passive "are called".

before: For a soul still growing towards its perfection, worship is the means of growth. For a soul that has reached perfection, worship is no longer for growth [@kernel, p. 30].
after: Where a soul still growing towards its perfection finds in worship the means of growth, a soul that has reached perfection no longer worships to grow [@kernel, p. 30].
note: Mirrored halves rewritten as one flowing sentence (the approved "Where…" shape).

before: What changes on arrival is not the law but the reason for keeping it.
after: What changes on arrival is the reason for keeping the law rather than the law itself.
note: "Not X but Y" → "rather than" (D53). The proponents' contrast is kept.

before: This chapter sets out why there is no path outside the law.
It is what the Prophet ﷺ taught us to do, and it is what most of us mean by practising the religion.
note: Mirrored "it is… it is" halves; vague "It" opener.

where: § The inner never cancels the outer, ¶3
before: The claim to know God fails without the law because of what the law does to the one who keeps it.
note: Abstract label sentence announcing the next step.

before: The question itself shows that the mind can be held, since a book holds it.
note: Abstract; "held… holds" echo; reads as a logic step.

before: The ʿurafaʾ describe it as four journeys: to God, in God, back from God to creation, and among creation.
note: List label after a colon; ranked most machine-like.

before: In the Sheikh's phrase, the last three are made "by the haqq", that is, through God, the Real, and not by the traveller's own strength.
note: Stacked glosses; "that is" gloss plus a "not" tail.
